open-question.question: `derive-tasks` and `submit-task` are to refresh the starting state when `since --milestones` prints a line beyond the anchor line. When it prints nothing at all, because the milestone has no `Starting-state:` commit (the step was skipped, or the section was written by hand or arrived in the milestone's first commit), does the writer follow the starting-state procedure as a first run and commit it, or go on to its own write with the section as it stands?
open-question.recommendation: The writers' check is the narrow one the design states, a print beyond the anchor line, so no anchor leaves nothing to measure from: a chain that left the step out, a hand-written section, and a seeded fixture are taken as they stand, the existing `submit-task` host test and the benchmark's ablation without the skill keep their meaning, and a first run stays the skill's.
open-question.alternative: When `since --milestones` prints nothing, the writer makes no starting-state commit and explores nothing. It goes on to its own reads and write with the `## Relevant starting state` section as it stands, empty or filled, and prints nothing about it. Only the skill reads no output as a first run. At task entry, no output simply means there is no anchor to measure from. It respects every reason the anchor is missing: a deliberately skipped step, the benchmark's ablation chain, a hand-written section, and the host fixture's seeded one. The writers stay cheap and their behaviour unchanged on such milestones, the existing `submit-task` host test included. The writer's only addition stays the narrow check the design draft states. The staleness check switches itself off for exactly the milestones that never ran the skill. A milestone whose section was hand-written or arrived in its first commit is never refreshed at task entry, even after a holder in its scope finished during the gate wait, which is the case the check exists for. A milestone that skipped the step entirely derives its tasks against an empty section, with nothing saying so.

When `since --milestones` prints nothing, `derive-tasks` and `submit-task` treat it like any stale state. Whatever the section holds, empty or filled, they follow the starting-state procedure as a first run. They edit the section in place by the procedure's one rule (a filled section's subsections whose facts still hold stay byte-identical), commit it as a commit of its own under `Starting-state: <path>`, and then go on to their own write with the section in hand. Nothing in the writer tells an empty section from a hand-written one, and no line is printed. One rule for every non-anchor print. A milestone reaching task entry by any route (a chain that left out the starting-state line, a hand-written section, a section that came in with the first commit) leaves the writer with an anchor in the log. Every later `since` check then has something to compare against, and the gate-wait refresh protects it like every other milestone. The refresh also stays never a stop, as the design draft requires. It puts the starting-state skill's work into a chain that deliberately left it out. The benchmark draft's ablation of a chain without the starting-state skill would explore and commit at `derive-tasks` anyway, and the host suite's existing `submit-task` test, run on the fixture milestone whose filled starting state came in with the seed commit and has no `Starting-state:` commit, would gain an exploration and an extra commit inside its 20-minute bound. If an exploration leaves a hand-written section byte-identical, no commit lands and no anchor appears, so every later entry explores again; how far that repeats depends on the "Unchanged refresh repeat" question. Which existing commits count as an anchor, and so how often this fires on a milestone kept in place by the migration, depends on the "Since anchor subject form" question.

When `since --milestones` prints nothing, the writer stops before its own write, with nothing changed. It prints a fixed, identifier-free line of its own (one per writer, each listed in the fixed-console-lines table), with a remedy below it naming `/specify-milestone-starting-state --milestone <path>`. The writer neither explores nor commits, and the check treats an empty section and a filled one alike. A missing anchor becomes visible, and the operator decides whether a hand-written or seeded section stands or gets a recorded first run. The writer never writes into the milestone's starting state on its own, and never derives against an unrecorded state without the operator having been told. It is a stop in a long unattended run for work the writer could do itself, which the design draft rules out for the stale case ("the refresh is never a stop"). It halts the benchmark's ablation chain at derivation, and it would stop the host suite's existing `submit-task` test on the fixture milestone unless that fixture gains a `Starting-state:` commit. It also adds two rows to the fixed-console-lines table and to `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py`'s check.

When `since --milestones` prints nothing, the writer looks at the `## Relevant starting state` section it is about to read. If the section holds no body under its heading, the writer follows the starting-state procedure as a first run, commits it under `Starting-state: <path>` as a commit of its own, and goes on. If the section holds anything, the writer takes it as it stands and goes on with no exploration and no commit. Nothing is printed in either case. No task is ever derived against an empty starting state. A section someone wrote by hand, or one seeded with the milestone's first commit like the host fixture's, is respected and costs nothing. The existing `submit-task` host test runs unchanged. A filled section without an anchor is still never refreshed after a gate wait, so the hand-written case keeps the staleness gap the check exists to close. The writer gains a content test on the section (what counts as empty) that the `since` print alone does not give it. The benchmark's ablation chain, whose section is empty, still gets the exploration at `derive-tasks`, which defeats that ablation.

When `since --milestones` prints nothing, the writer looks at the `## Relevant starting state` section. If the section holds no body under its heading, the writer stops before its own write on a fixed line of its own, with nothing changed and a remedy naming `/specify-milestone-starting-state --milestone <path>`. If the section holds anything, the writer takes it as it stands and goes on with no exploration and no commit. The writer never runs an exploration on a milestone that never had one and never derives against an empty section. A hand-written or seeded section is respected with no cost. This keeps every write of the starting state either with the skill or with a refresh of an anchor that already exists. It is still a stop in an unattended run, for a case the writer could handle itself, and it halts the benchmark's ablation chain at derivation. The filled-but-unanchored section keeps the staleness gap after a gate wait. It also needs both the section-content test and new fixed-line rows for the two writers.

When the milestone has no `Starting-state:` commit, the staleness test measures from a stand-in anchor instead: the commit that added the milestone's `requirements.md` (its `Milestone-definition:` commit, or whatever first commit brought the file in). The writer reaches that commit through a fallback in the milestones tool's `since` query or a sibling form of it, still a log read. If an empty section has no anchor, the writer always follows the procedure as a first run. If a filled section has no anchor, the writer follows the procedure in place, and commits under `Starting-state: <path>`, only when other milestones' task or finish commits landed after the stand-in. Otherwise it goes on with the section as it stands. A hand-written or seeded section gets the same protection after a gate wait as an anchored one, without an exploration on every entry: the writer refreshes only when the ground has actually moved since the milestone existed. An empty section is never derived against. The existing `submit-task` host test runs unchanged, since nothing has moved in the fixture's one-commit history. It changes the `since` contract, under which no output means no starting state, or adds a second query form. The procedure's three-outcome opening gains a fourth outcome, and the tool's docs and tests grow with it. The stand-in can be older than a section written by hand later, so it may fire on ground the hand-written section already described. The benchmark's ablation chain still gets the first-run exploration at `derive-tasks`, because its section is empty.

open-question.question: `derive-tasks` and `submit-task` check the scope gate directly ahead of their write call today, after their reads and their authoring. The staleness check has to follow the gate and precede those reads, which moves the gate to the front of each writer. Is the gate then checked once, at the front, or again directly before the write call as well, now that the reads, a possible refresh, and the authoring stand between the check and the write?
open-question.recommendation: The second check keeps today's one-turn window between the gate and the write now that the reads, a possible exploration, and the authoring follow the front check; two overlapping milestones started inside that window block each other's completion with no light recovery, since started is read from the log, and the cost is one cheap call per run under an unconditional rule.
open-question.alternative: In both writers the scope gate runs twice, each time as its own step following `check-scope-gate.md`: once at the front, directly after resolution and before the staleness check, reads, refresh, and authoring, and again directly ahead of the fixed write call, where it stands today, on every run. Either check closing stops the run under the procedure's one fixed line with nothing further written; a refresh commit that already landed before a closed second check stays committed. `derive-tasks`' no-brief run skips the second check as it skips the write; the fixed write calls stay gate-free. Keeps today's one-turn window between the gate and the write while gaining the front check the refresh ordering needs, so an overlapping holder that starts during the reads, exploration, or authoring is refused at entry rather than surfacing later as two started milestones blocking each other's completion; the rule is unconditional, with no branch to state or test. Two gate calls and two references to the shared procedure per writer, the second paid on every run even though a holder starting inside one run's window has not yet happened on this repository; a run whose second check closes after an inline refresh leaves that `Starting-state:` commit landed and stops, so the rerun once the holder finishes explores again, the holder's finish commit lying beyond the new anchor.

In both `derive-tasks` and `submit-task` the scope gate moves to the front of the workflow as its own step, directly after milestone resolution and before the `since --milestones` staleness check, the reads, any inline refresh, and the authoring. It is checked there once per run and not again: the step that today stands directly ahead of the fixed write call (`derive-tasks` step 7, `submit-task` step 5) is removed, and the write call follows the authoring (and `derive-tasks`' plan presentation) with no gate between them. The writers' fixed write calls stay gate-free, and each skill's Preconditions line names the one front step. One gate call per writer and one place each writer can print the gate's fixed stop line, matching the design draft's single ordering rule (the gate first, then the staleness check) with no duplicated step; the overlap this leaves open is the one the invariants already assign to the completion-site gates, which `complete-all-tasks` and `complete-task` run before every task to catch a list written after another milestone's entry check ran. The window between the check and the write grows from one turn today to the reads, a possible exploration and its `Starting-state:` commit, the authoring, and in `derive-tasks` the plan presentation the user may interrupt, so a holder that starts in an overlapping scope during that time is not seen at entry; both milestones then stand started, and each one's completion gate stops on the other until one of them is finished, a heavier recovery than an entry refusal. A `derive-tasks` run that derives no brief also now meets the gate, and can stop on it, where today it skips the gate.

In both writers the scope gate runs at the front as its own step, directly after resolution and before the staleness check, and runs again as its own step directly ahead of the fixed write call only when the run's staleness check fired and the writer followed the starting-state procedure inline; a run whose state was fresh goes from its authoring to the write call with no second check. The fixed write calls stay gate-free. Pays the second gate call only on the runs where the longest step, an exploration and its commit, stood between the check and the write, and where the scope has just been shown to be moving; in the documented chains, which refresh before task entry, that is the rare hand-built chain, merge, or re-entry after a gate wait. Adds a branch to each writer's step list keyed on whether the refresh ran, which the writer must carry from the staleness step to the write; a fresh-state run still keeps the reads, the authoring, and `derive-tasks`' interruptible plan presentation between check and write, so the window the other two-check option closes stays open there. What counts as a refresh having run depends on the sibling question of whether a milestone with no `Starting-state:` anchor gets a first-run exploration inline.

alternative.id: Front step, re-check in write call

open-question.alternative: In both writers the scope gate runs at the front as its own step, directly after resolution and before the staleness check, and is checked again inside the fixed write call itself: the call opens with the milestones tool's `gate <MILESTONE_DIR>` and an empty-output test chained ahead of the task-list tool's `initialize` or `insert` behind `&&`, so a held scope or failed check writes and commits nothing. The before-write gate step is removed, and the invariant that the entry writers' fixed calls carry no gate is reversed for these two calls. Shrinks the window between the last check and the write to the same shell process, closer than today's one turn, without adding a turn per run, so an overlapping holder is refused at entry in every case short of a start inside that one call. Reverses a recorded invariant (the gate is a step of its own, never a test inside the write calls) and splits the gate between the shared procedure and two fixed calls: the closed-gate fixed line and the holder paths or `Error:` line beneath it must be printed by the call, or the call's output translated back into the procedure's report, a second home for the procedure's stop and two more fixed calls whose fixed-call tests must cover the gate's branches.

open-question.question: The review pass is to read the `milestones` overview on its milestone's scope, bounded to the recent milestones, on every pass, but the `milestones` query takes no bound today and prints every milestone that ever touched the scope (56 lines on this repository's root). How is that overview bounded to the recent ones?
open-question.recommendation: A fixed count of the newest finished lines beside every live line is the plain reading of recent, keeps the print the same size on every pass of the loop, still shows a recently finished milestone the starting state did not weigh, and needs neither the anchor nor the clock.
open-question.alternative: The bound is a count, applied in the tool: `milestones` gains an optional flag (for example `--last N`) that keeps every live line and only the N newest finished lines, by finish timestamp, the order the query already sorts them in. The review pass's one fixed call writes N as a literal (on the order of ten). Without the flag the query prints what it prints today, so `record`, `/release-plugin`, and every other reader are unchanged. The overview's size is fixed whatever the project's age or pace, so a pass repeated until convergence pays the same small print every time. It is the simplest rule to state, test on a temporary repository, and read, and it needs nothing from the starting state's anchor or from the clock. N is arbitrary and blind to the milestone: on a busy scope a milestone finished just before the starting state was written can already have fallen off, and on a quiet one the N lines reach back years past anything relevant. It adds a flag to a query whose contract the CLAUDE.md invariant spells out, so that invariant and the help text change with it.

The bound is a time window, applied in the tool: `milestones` gains an optional flag (for example `--within DAYS`) that keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit's author date falls within that many days of today. The review pass's fixed call writes the day count as a literal. "Recent" is read in its plain sense, as calendar time, so a burst of finishes all shows and a long-quiet scope prints only its live lines, and the window needs no milestone-specific anchor or count tuned to the project's milestone size. The print depends on the clock and the project's pace rather than on the milestone: a milestone that sits deciding for longer than the window loses sight of what finished just before its starting state, a dormant project sees nothing at all, and a fast one can print as much as the unbounded query. The tool's tests must pin "today", which none of its queries does now.

The bound is relative to the milestone itself, applied in the tool: the query (by a flag on `milestones`, given the milestone's path) keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit is newer than the milestone's own latest `Starting-state:` commit, the anchor the new `since` query finds, falling back to the unbounded list when the milestone has no anchor yet. On a fresh or freshly refreshed state the finished part is usually empty. It prints exactly the complement of what the starting state already carries, the milestones finished since it was written, on a branch merged in the meantime included, so the overview never repeats the starting state and stays near empty on every pass of a loop whose ground has not moved. It reuses the anchor lookup `since` needs anyway. A milestone finished before the anchor that the starting-state read did not weigh, the third case the draft gives the overview for, is never shown, so the pass relies wholly on the starting state's judgment for everything older. It needs the milestone's path rather than a scope, a condition on the scope-argument question, and inherits whatever the anchor-subject question settles about which `Starting-state:` commits count.

The bound is relative to the milestone itself, applied in the tool: the query (by a flag on `milestones`, given the milestone's path) keeps every live line and only the finished milestones whose finish commit is newer than the milestone's own `Milestone-definition:` commit, a point that never moves once the milestone exists. The window is stable for the milestone's whole life and needs no starting-state anchor, so it is independent of how the `since` anchor is matched and of whether a refresh ran, and it still shows everything that finished while this milestone was being prepared. After a refresh it keeps listing milestones the refreshed starting state has already absorbed, so the overview grows with the milestone's age rather than with what is new; like the anchor form it hides older milestones the starting state did not weigh. A live milestone kept in place by the migration may carry a definition subject naming a bare directory rather than its path, so the tool needs a rule for finding it, and it takes the milestone's path, a condition on the scope-argument question.

The bound combines the milestone-relative and count forms, applied in the tool: the query keeps every live line and the finished milestones that are either newer than the milestone's latest `Starting-state:` commit or among the N newest finished ones, whichever set is larger, N written as a literal in the review pass's fixed call. It shows everything new since the starting state however many that is, and still keeps a short tail of the most recent older milestones in view, so the case of a recently finished milestone the starting-state read did not weigh is covered as well as the post-anchor one. It is the most complex rule to state, test, and explain, two bounds and a union where one would do, and it still hides anything older than the tail. It shares the anchor form's dependence on the milestone's path and on how the anchor subject is matched, both questions owned by siblings.

The bound is a count applied in the runner, not the tool: the review pass's fixed call pipes the unchanged `milestones` query on its scope through `head -n N`, N a literal, so the first N lines, the live ones first and then the newest finished, are what the pass reads. The tool and its contract do not change. No tool change, no new flag, no new tests or invariant text for the milestones tool: the bound is one fixed literal in one skill file, trivially adjusted later. Live lines eat the count, so a scope with many live milestones shows fewer finished ones; and the pipe's exit status is `head`'s, so a refused or failed tool call reads as success with an empty or partial overview unless the call adds `pipefail` or a separate test, which bears on the read-failure question. A shell filter on tool output is the kind of per-site hand-rolled step the tools exist to replace.

The premise that the overview is bounded is rejected: the review pass's fixed call reads the unchanged `milestones` query on its scope whole, every live and every finished milestone that touched it, one line each (56 lines, about 5 KB, on this repository's root today), and the pass's own judgment picks which lines bear. Nothing is ever hidden, the older milestone the starting state did not weigh included, and no tool change, flag, or bound value has to be chosen, tested, or later re-tuned; it is the query exactly as `/release-plugin` and `record` already rely on. The print grows by one line per milestone forever and is paid again on every pass of a loop that runs until convergence, the cost the draft bounds the overview to avoid; on a root-scoped project every milestone the project ever finished is listed, most of them irrelevant, which dilutes the pass's attention.

open-question.question: The review pass gains one fixed call to the milestones tool at its inventory step, the `milestones` overview. When that call fails (the tool refuses, or git is unavailable), does the pass stop on a fixed line of its own before changing anything, or report the failure and carry on reviewing from the milestone's two documents alone?
open-question.recommendation: The pass writes and commits, so a failed fixed history read is one unclassified stop, as it is for finish and both task-entry writers; a harness looping to the verdict never takes a pass that skipped the record for convergence, and since the call fails almost only where the pass's own commit would fail too, stopping first costs nothing and leaves no reshaped document uncommitted.
open-question.alternative: A failed overview call (any non-zero exit, the tool's `Error:` line or git's failure alike, treated as one condition and never classified by its wording) stops the pass at its inventory step, before any prune, dedup, new block, or note deletion. The pass prints one new fixed, identifier-free stop line of its own as its report's first line with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim beneath it. It makes no commit and prints neither the still-open list nor the convergence verdict. The new line gets its row in the `## Fixed console lines` table. A harness looping the review until the verdict line sees a stop, not a convergence formed without the record, and the overview stays as unconditional as the design meant ("whether to look is never the pass's choice"). It follows the precedent of the other fixed history reads in skills that write and commit: `finish-milestone` and `derive-tasks` stop on their own line when `tasks` or `list` fails. Stopping costs almost nothing extra in practice. On a scope directory that exists, `milestones PATH` refuses only when git cannot be run or its output cannot be read, and in that case the pass's own step-5 commit through the commit tool would fail too. Stopping first avoids leaving a reshaped `open_questions.xml` uncommitted behind a failed commit. It adds a stop line, a table row, and a review stop that every chain's harness must recognise. Any failure of a read that only feeds the pass's judgment blocks the requirements loop entirely, even though the two documents alone would still let the pass reconcile and surface most gaps. The same holds for a refusal introduced by a later change to the call's arguments (the bound is a sibling's to set): it stops every pass on every milestone until fixed.

A failed overview call does not stop the pass. It goes on through reconciliation, gap surfacing, the decision consistency check, and its commit, using `requirements.md` and `open_questions.xml` alone. Its report keeps its usual fixed first line (`Requirements reviewed.` or the no-op line). Below that line it adds one advisory saying the milestones overview could not be read, with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim, beside the still-open list. The convergence verdict is printed exactly as today, whenever the closing `list` prints nothing. No new fixed line is added. The loop engine keeps doing its core job on a read that only complements the starting state, which is how the conversational readers treat a failed history read (`ask-in-milestone-context` tells it in prose and carries on). The fixed-lines table, the verdict's contract, and every chain's expected lines stay unchanged. A harness matching the verdict leaves the loop on a pass that never saw the record. The overview exists to catch exactly one case, a milestone finished since the starting state or merged in from a branch, and that case then reaches task derivation unflagged, with the advisory visible only to a human reading the message. It also adds a new advisory kind to the short list of decision-critical advisories. When git itself is the failure, the pass carries on only to fail at its step-5 commit, leaving its edits uncommitted.

A failed overview call does not stop the pass. It reconciles, surfaces gaps, checks decisions against each other, and commits from the two documents alone, keeping its usual fixed first line and adding one advisory below it with the `Error:` line quoted verbatim. On such a pass the convergence verdict line is never printed, even when the closing `list` prints nothing, and the still-open list is reported as usual. The pass still does all the reshaping work the two documents allow. A harness looping until the verdict does not take a review that skipped the record for a converged one, so a degraded pass can never send the milestone on to task derivation. The verdict now carries a second condition, which breaks its listed contract of being printed whenever `list` prints nothing. Its documentation and its fixed-lines test semantics would have to change. A loop whose overview keeps failing re-runs the review until the harness's own cap, never converging and never showing a stop line that names why. When git itself is the failure, the step-5 commit fails anyway.

open-question.question: Each of the three chains on the ways-of-using page that derive and complete tasks ("Answering the questions that matter to you", "Putting more intelligence into a stuck milestone", "Executing tasks") is to open with the refresh line and one review pass. A question that review raises needs an alternatives line, a recommend line, and an answer line before `derive-tasks` will run, and two of the three chains carry no alternatives line today. What lines does each of those chains carry between its opening review and its derivation line?
open-question.recommendation: It is the smallest set that lets derivation run whenever the opening review raised questions, keeps every chain a straight list of complete invocations, and matches the rigour the Executing tasks chain has today, deriving directly behind a sweep; on unmoved ground the added lines end on their no-op lines, so the chain pays the `since` call and one converged review.
open-question.alternative: Each chain carries exactly one alternatives line, one recommend line, and one sweep line between the opening review and derivation, in that order, and nothing after the sweep. "Executing tasks" gains the alternatives and recommend lines ahead of its sweep. "Answering the questions that matter to you" gains an alternatives line after its hand-answer lines and ahead of its existing recommend line. "Putting more intelligence into a stuck milestone" keeps its own alternatives, recommend, and sweep lines as that pass. The new lines take the model and effort settings the "Starting a milestone" chain gives them. It is the smallest set that lets derivation run whenever the opening review raised questions: every new question gets a set, a pick, and a recorded answer, so `derive-tasks` finds the document empty. On unmoved ground, the alternatives and recommend lines end on their fixed no-op lines at little cost. The chains stay straight lists of complete invocations, as the page's notation describes. No review runs after the sweep, so derivation goes ahead on decisions just recorded without anyone weighing them against each other or against the refreshed facts. A question one of those answers opens is first surfaced only by a later review, if one ever runs. This is one pass, not the loop to convergence the draft names. In "Answering the questions that matter to you", the questions the opening review raises are answered by the sweep, not by the person at the keyboard, who never read them.

Between the opening review and the derivation line each chain keeps only the lines it carries today, with no pass added. "Answering the questions that matter to you" keeps its answer lines, its recommend line, and its sweep line. "Executing tasks" keeps its one sweep line. "Putting more intelligence into a stuck milestone" keeps its own alternatives, recommend, and sweep lines. When the opening review raises a question, `derive-tasks` stops on its precondition line with that question listed, and the operator runs the "Running a mixed-agent requirements review" chain before re-entering. The chain paragraphs say so. Adds the fewest lines and costs no extra run. On ground that did not move, the opening review converges and derivation proceeds exactly as today. When the ground moved, the review raises a question, and that bare question stops the chain at derivation. In "Answering the questions that matter to you" it also stops the recommend line on `Recommendation pass stopped — some questions lack alternatives.` The draft rules out exactly this stop ("the refresh is never a stop"). It would hand the operator a chain to run in the middle of an unattended execution, and it does not give the "standard loop to convergence" that the draft's "Where the refresh runs" paragraph promises.

Each chain carries the one completing pass (alternatives, recommend, and sweep lines placed in each chain as in the one-pass option) followed by a second review line directly ahead of derivation. If that closing review raises a question, `derive-tasks` stops on its precondition line and the operator runs the mixed-agent review chain. Derivation never runs on a set of decisions that a review has not seen after the last sweep. If the sweep's answers opened something, the chain stops at a visible, listed question instead of deriving tasks past it. Every run pays a second review at the review line's effort, even on unmoved ground where that review only confirms convergence. A sweep that opens a question still turns into a stop at derivation in the middle of execution, which is the stop the refresh was designed to avoid. The chain is still bounded at two reviews, not run to convergence.

Each chain writes out the full pass (alternatives, recommend, sweep, then another review) a fixed number of times, two or more, between the opening review and derivation. The count is the same in all three chains, and each chain's existing lines fill the first pass's places as in the one-pass option. Every pass after a converged review runs to its fixed no-op lines. It gets close to convergence without leaving the page's notation. Every line is still a complete invocation separated by `;`, and the derivation stop is rarer the more passes are written out. Each chain grows by four lines per pass, and every pass runs even after convergence, paying a review and three no-op passes each time. The count is arbitrary, and if a milestone needs more passes than were written out, the chain still stops at derivation. A long repeated block also makes the three chains harder to read and keep in step with each other.

Between the opening review and derivation each chain carries one bounded shell loop that runs the alternatives, recommend, and sweep lines and then another review. It exits when a review's final message holds the fixed line `Requirements converged — ready for task derivation.`, matched as a whole line in that run's output, or after a fixed count of passes. In "Answering the questions that matter to you" the hand-answer lines and an added alternatives line come before the loop. In "Putting more intelligence into a stuck milestone" the loop takes that chain's own settings. The page's notation section gains a description of the loop construct. This is the "standard loop to convergence" the draft names. It mirrors the benchmark's bounded `review` loop, whose exit signal is that same fixed line, and it uses the convergence line for the purpose the fixed-line contract gives it. Converged ground exits after the first check, and moved ground gets as many review passes as it needs, up to the bound. It breaks the page's rule that every chain line is one complete invocation, adding shell control flow the page has never carried. That control flow has to read each host CLI's printed final message from stdout, which works differently on each of the three hosts and must be written per host. A milestone that does not converge within the bound still reaches the derivation stop, and the loop's syntax is one more thing a hand-built chain can get wrong.

open-question.question: The benchmark draft's two cairn deliveries each run one unbroken chain per phase: the starting-state line, the bounded review loop, then the derivation line directly behind the loop. Once every execution chain on the ways-of-using page opens with the refresh line and a review pass, do the benchmark deliveries gain a second starting-state line ahead of their derivation line, or keep the one they have?
open-question.recommendation: The existing line already stands where the rule puts the refresh, directly ahead of the first review, and in a single-milestone run nothing outside the milestone's directory lands before derivation, so a second line would only add an always-no-op invocation and raise the control's N; saying so once where the chain is defined keeps a later sync to the docs from adding it back.
open-question.alternative: Both cairn deliveries keep their one starting-state line in place and their lists unchanged, as in the first option. The draft's chain text gains one statement of why: the existing line already stands where the ways-of-using rule puts the refresh, directly ahead of the first review pass, and in a single-milestone run nothing outside the milestone's directory lands between it and derivation, so a second line would end on the no-op line every time. The expected-lines list takes the new no-op line from the table as before. Keeps every benefit of the unchanged list (no extra invocation, an unchanged N for the multi-prompt control, unchanged K, an unchanged ablation) and records the departure from the ways-of-using chains where the chain is defined, so a later sync of the draft to the docs does not add the line back by mistake. The draft takes on a claim about how `since` behaves that has to be re-checked whenever the starting-state procedure or the benchmark's scenarios change (for example a scenario that runs a second milestone, or a step that commits outside the milestone directory). That is one more sentence of reasoning in an 807-line draft, and it can go stale.

Both cairn deliveries, `cairn_<version>_yolo` and `cairn_<version>_assess_answers_manually`, keep the one starting-state line where it stands, after the definition line and ahead of the bounded review loop, with the derivation line directly behind the loop. Neither list gains a line, and the draft adds no text about the ways-of-using rule. The only change the milestone makes for the starting-state line is the expected-lines list in "Detecting a stop", which takes the skill's new no-op line from the fixed-lines table along with its other lines. Every list, the invocation count N the multi-prompt control copies, the loop's K semantics, and the `no_starting_state` ablation stay exactly as they are. Nothing is lost by keeping them: in a single-milestone run, phase 1 or phase 2 (milestone 1 is already finished when milestone 2 is defined), every commit between the starting-state commit and derivation (review, annotation, and answer commits, and the assess turn's answers) changes only the milestone's own files. A second line would therefore always print the anchor alone and end on the no-op line, and the derivation line's own `since --milestones` check never fires. The benchmark's chains then differ silently from the rule the ways-of-using page states, that every execution chain opens with the refresh line and a review pass. A later reader or editor syncing the draft to that page may take the gap for an oversight and "fix" it, and the benchmark never runs the documented chain shape in which the new no-op line is printed.

Both cairn deliveries gain a second `/cairn:specify-milestone-starting-state --milestone <path>` line outside the bounded loop, directly ahead of `/cairn:derive-tasks`. The list then runs: the first starting-state line, the loop, the refresh line, derivation. The loop and the operator's planned turn are unchanged, and no extra review line is added. The refresh line's expected lines are the skill's success line and both of its no-op lines, the new one included, copied from the table like every other line's. The benchmark exercises the shipped refresh at the point the documented execution chains put it, so the cost the real chains pay for it (one invocation and one `since` call) is part of what is measured. In every run it is also a live check on the new no-op line: a refresh that explores, or ends on no expected line, where nothing moved shows up in the record as a stop or as an unexpected `Starting-state:` commit. It adds one headless invocation per phase per run, and in a single-milestone run it always ends on the no-op line. It raises N for the multi-prompt control mirrored from it, makes the lists of this version differ in length from those of earlier releases being compared, and means the `no_starting_state` ablation must now drop two lines. There is no second loop, since a delivery holds at most one bounded loop. The list then runs: the first starting-state line, the loop, the refresh line, one review line, derivation. Both added lines take their skills' expected lines from the table. The deliveries match the documented chains as closely as the one-loop rule allows, so what the benchmark scores is the execution shape Cairn tells its users to run, review after refresh included, and a reader can compare the two without making allowance for any difference. It adds two invocations per phase per run, both redundant in a single-milestone run: the refresh always ends on its no-op line, and the review repeats the loop's last pass. It can also change outcomes as well as cost. A review standing outside the loop that raises a question, or that follows a loop which ran out of K passes, has no alternatives, recommendation, or answer line behind it, so derivation stops on the open question where the loop's exit would otherwise have gone straight on. It also raises the multi-prompt control's N by two and changes what the `no_starting_state` ablation has to drop.

open-question.question: The host-suite test needs `derive-tasks` to find its milestone's scope free and its starting state stale, which takes a second, overlapping milestone whose task or finish commits land after the first milestone's `Starting-state:` commit and which no longer holds the scope when `derive-tasks` runs. Is that second milestone seeded as already finished in the seeded repository's history, or left live in the seed and finished through the host by the test before it derives?
open-question.recommendation: One headless run against a history the test fixes itself keeps a failure pointing at `derive-tasks`' gate, `since --milestones`, and refresh path alone, on each of three hosts under a 20-minute bound, and leaves the shared seed and the existing tests untouched; the finish commit's form is the tool tests' to pin.
open-question.alternative: The second milestone reaches the host already finished. Test-side code, local to the new test (a helper or seeding variant beside the unchanged `seeded_repo`), builds the history on top of the seed in this order: the first milestone's `Starting-state: <path>` commit, then the second, overlapping milestone's files added, its `Task-completion:` commits, and its `Milestone-finish: <path>` commit removing its directory, made through the plugin's commit tool. Only one host process runs, `/cairn:derive-tasks --milestone …`. The shared one-commit seed, and the other host tests that use it, are left as they are. Exactly one headless run, against a history whose subjects, order, and removal the test fixes itself, so a failure points at `derive-tasks`' gate-then-`since --milestones`-then-refresh path alone and not at another skill's run. The existing `submit-task` test's seed is unchanged. The holder's finish is written by hand, not by `finish-milestone`, so the test can pass on a finish commit (subject, body, removal) that the plugin would never produce, and the gate-wait-then-open sequence the design names is never run. The helper also has to keep the second milestone's fixture files somewhere the discovery pattern does not match until it adds them.

The second milestone reaches the host already finished, as in the test-local form, but the multi-commit history (first milestone's `Starting-state:` anchor, then the second milestone's task commits and its `Milestone-finish:` removal) is built by the shared `seeded_repo` from an extended fixture project. Every host test therefore starts from that history. The new test runs only `/cairn:derive-tasks` through the host. Every host test then runs against one realistic multi-milestone history in one place, with no second seeding path to maintain, and the refresh test still costs one headless run. Changes the ground under the existing tests. `test_plugin_root_resolution.py`'s `submit-task` run would meet a finished overlapping milestone and could refresh inline, or not, depending on whether its milestone has an anchor (the axis "No anchor at task entry" owns), so an unrelated test's behaviour and run time change. The finish is still hand-made, as in the test-local form.

The seed's history holds the first milestone's `Starting-state:` commit and then the second, overlapping milestone live and started, its tasks already completed by seeded `Task-completion:` commits made after that anchor, with an empty question document and no section left in its task list. The test runs `/cairn:finish-milestone --milestone <second>` through the host and then `/cairn:derive-tasks --milestone <first>` through the host: two headless runs. The `Milestone-finish:` commit that `since --milestones` reads, and the gate's opening, both come from the plugin itself. The test covers the case the design names, a milestone re-entered at derivation once its holder finished, against a finish commit the plugin really writes. Doubles the headless cost (two runs, each bounded at 20 minutes) and puts the refresh assertion behind a `finish-milestone` run that can fail or vary for reasons of its own on any of the three hosts, such as whether it edits a context file the fixture lacks. The task commits are still hand-seeded.

alternative.id: Live holder, host completes and finishes

open-question.alternative: The seed's history holds the first milestone's `Starting-state:` commit and then the second, overlapping milestone live and started with one pending task. Through the host, the test runs `/cairn:complete-task` on that task, then `/cairn:finish-milestone` on the second milestone, then `/cairn:derive-tasks` on the first: three headless runs. Every commit after the anchor is made by the plugin. No commit `since --milestones` reads is hand-made: both the `Task-completion:` and the `Milestone-finish:` commits come from the runners that make them in real use, so drift in either subject form shows up in this test. Three headless runs per host make it the costliest and least deterministic arrangement. A task completion has open-ended work in it, and a failure in either earlier skill fails the refresh test, even though the finish commit alone already makes the state stale.

open-question.question: The new host-suite test is to assert the refresh on all three hosts, but the suite runs on demand, outside CI, and can pass on a host only after the rebuilt tree is committed and that host's installed plugin copy is refreshed by hand. Does completing this milestone require a passing run of the test against each of the three hosts, the task that runs it refreshing the installed copies first, or only that the test is delivered and passes on the hosts available when it lands?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The goal asserts the refresh on all three hosts and the contributor guide owes a passing run on each for a `host_tests/` change, and the suite's own milestone showed the path works on this machine: all three CLIs are installed and its tasks refreshed each installed copy and passed the suite on 2026-11-09, so the claim is verified before the milestone's directory and context are gone.
open-question.alternative: Completion requires a passing run of the whole host suite, the new test included, against each of the three hosts (`--host claude`, `--host antigravity`, `--host codex`). The task that runs it starts, once the rebuilt tree is committed, by refreshing each host's installed copy on the maintainer's machine with that host's documented install, as the host-generic suite milestone's "Refreshing installed copies" decision has its suite-running tasks do. A host that fails is fixed inside this milestone before it finishes. It verifies the goal's "on all three hosts" claim before the milestone closes and meets the rule CONTRIBUTING.md already sets, that a change under `host_tests/` owes a passing run on all three hosts before it is committed, following the precedent the sibling suite milestone recorded. The milestone cannot finish without all three CLIs installed and working on the maintainer's machine, up to three 20-minute headless runs, and a task runner writing into `~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn`, `~/.codex/plugins/cache/`, and Claude Code's plugin install, which may prompt for permission or fail in an unattended `complete-all-tasks` run. A host integration defect the new test exposes becomes this milestone's work and holds its finish.

Completion requires a passing run against each of the three hosts, as above, but no task refreshes an installed copy: the maintainer brings each copy up to date by hand outside the task run, and the task that runs the suite stops with its tree left resumable on the suite's `host suite prerequisite missing:` line for any host whose copy is stale, to be resumed once the copy is refreshed. A host that fails is fixed inside this milestone. It keeps the full three-host verification while no agent run of this workflow writes to any installation outside the repository, extending the suite's own no-write-to-installations rule to the runner that drives it. The task that runs the suite cannot complete in one unattended pass: it needs a human step between the rebuilt tree's commit and the run, so a headless chain stops there and the milestone waits on the maintainer, and it carries the same CLI-availability and host-defect costs as the task-refresh form.

Completion requires that the test is delivered and passes on each host whose CLI is installed on the maintainer's machine when the task runs. The task refreshes those hosts' installed copies first, and a host whose CLI is absent is not run, its run left to the release pre-flight's check g, which selects all three hosts because `host_tests/` changed. A host that is run and fails is fixed inside this milestone. A missing CLI on the maintainer's machine never blocks the milestone, while every host that can be run is still verified before finish. It falls short of CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule for a `host_tests/` change, and the goal's three-host claim may stand unverified on a host until the next release, where a failure found by check g stops the release outside any milestone.

Completion requires that the test is delivered and passes on each host whose installed copy already matches the committed built tree when the task runs, with no installed copy refreshed by the task or required of the maintainer. In practice that is the Claude Code install reading from the checkout's `hosts/claude/` through the directory marketplace, whose freshness check passes trivially; every other host is left to the release pre-flight's check g. It needs no write to any installation and no human step, so the task completes unattended while still running the new test end to end on at least the host that loads straight from the checkout. It verifies at most one host before finish, falling short of both the goal's three-host assertion and CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule, and leaves Antigravity and Codex behaviour, the hosts whose integrations most often differed, to be discovered at release.

The task refreshes all three installed copies and runs the suite against each host, but completion requires only that the three runs are made and their outcomes recorded, not that every one passes: a host failing for a defect in that host's integration rather than in this milestone's refresh behaviour is recorded as a follow-up (a task submitted to a later milestone, or a note in that host's `settings.toml` hands-on block) and does not hold the finish, while a failure of the refresh behaviour itself is fixed here. Every host is exercised before finish and nothing is left undiscovered, while a host-specific integration defect unrelated to the starting-state refresh cannot keep this milestone from closing. It ships a test known to fail on a host, so `main` would fail CONTRIBUTING.md's pre-commit rule for that host and the next release's check g until the follow-up lands, and telling a host integration defect from a refresh defect is a judgment made at run time with no fixed test.

Completion requires only that the test is written and committed with the rebuilt trees, with no host run as part of the milestone and no installed copy refreshed by it. Its first runs are the release pre-flight's check g, which selects all three hosts because `host_tests/` changed since the last release, and any failure there is handled outside this milestone. The milestone completes entirely from the repository and the automated tool tests, with no external CLI, no write to any installation, and no 20-minute headless runs, while the release gate already guarantees the test runs on all three hosts before anything ships. The test's correctness is unproven when the milestone finishes, it breaks CONTRIBUTING.md's rule that a `host_tests/` change owes a passing run on all three hosts before it is committed, and a fault in the test or in the refresh it asserts surfaces at release time, after the milestone's directory and context are gone.

open-question.question: In a shallow clone the truncated log can omit a milestone's `Starting-state:` commit, so the new `since` query would read a recorded starting state as never written. Does `since` refuse a shallow repository as `gate` does, or read whatever the log yields with the limit stated only in its help text, as the history queries do?
open-question.recommendation: `since` opens a procedure whose commit becomes the anchor and whose record read the design rests its protection on, so one refusal there keeps a truncated log from reading as no starting state or grounding a committed section, at no practical cost since the gate already refuses a shallow clone at task entry.
open-question.alternative: `since` runs the same `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` test `gate` runs (the existing `is_shallow()` helper), before any log read and in both forms, the broad one and `--milestones`, and refuses on `true` with one `Error:` line naming `git fetch --unshallow` as the remedy, whatever the truncated log would have yielded. Its help text and the milestones-tool invariant then name two queries that check, `gate` and `since`, in place of "only `gate`". `since` is the starting-state procedure's opening call, so one refusal there stops the whole procedure before anything is read: a shallow clone can then neither report a recorded starting state as never written nor go on to the later `milestones` and `summary` reads, which the same truncated log would also make silently incomplete, and write a section grounded in a partial record. The case costs nothing at the task-entry writers, which check `gate` first and so already stop in a shallow clone before `since --milestones` runs; the check reuses a helper and a message the tool already has. It also refuses the shallow clones where the answer would have been right, any clone deep enough to hold the anchor, so `specify-milestone-starting-state` cannot run at all in a shallow checkout (a CI-style `--depth` clone, for instance) until it is unshallowed, and it widens a rule the third milestone settled as `gate` alone checking. What the skill does with the `Error:` line (a fixed stop line, or going on without the read) is the "Starting-state read failure" question's to settle.

`since` reads the log first and runs the shallow test only when it found no `Starting-state:` anchor for the milestone's `requirements.md`, refusing then with the same `Error:` line and `git fetch --unshallow` remedy; when the anchor was found it prints its lines as usual in a shallow clone and a complete one alike. The refusal applies to both forms, and the help text states that a shallow clone is refused only where the missing anchor might be truncation. It refuses exactly the one output the question names as wrong: a found anchor and every commit after it are newer than the anchor and so present in the truncated log, which makes those lines trustworthy, while "no line" is the only answer a shallow clone can falsify. A shallow clone deep enough to hold the anchor keeps working, and nothing is refused that would have been read correctly by `since` itself. The query's behaviour now depends on what it found as well as on the repository, a second code path and a refusal rule harder to state in one help-text sentence than either uniform form, and the protection ends at `since`: on a found anchor the procedure goes on to the `milestones` and `summary` reads, which the truncated log can still leave incomplete with no sign, so a refresh in a shallow clone may still miss older milestones. What the skill does on the refusal is the "Starting-state read failure" question's to settle.

`since` gets no shallow check: it prints whatever the truncated path-scoped log yields, with no stop line and no warning, exactly as `tasks`, `milestones`, `summary`, and `record` do, and its help text and the docs state the limit (a shallow clone can omit the anchor, which then reads as no starting state written). `gate` stays the one query that checks, and the invariant's "only `gate`" stands unchanged. It keeps the tool's settled split, `gate` alone checking because a gate passing silently lets two runs collide while a history reader wants what is there, and adds no code, no refusal, and no failure for any runner to handle. The missed anchor is mild in effect: the task-entry writers never reach `since` in a shallow clone because `gate` refuses first, and in `specify-milestone-starting-state` a missed anchor only turns a refresh or a no-op into a first run, which edits the section in place, leaving byte-identical every subsection whose facts still hold, and lands a new `Starting-state:` commit that becomes the anchor from then on. In a shallow clone the skill misreads a recorded starting state as never written with no sign to anyone, pays an exploration the no-op line would have spared, and may write prose for unchanged facts that the next review pass reads as change; the later record reads it explores with are truncated just as silently, so the refreshed section can be grounded in a partial history and nothing tells the operator to unshallow.
